1:
Matthew Henry opens with the alchemists who sought the philosophers’ stone and never found it, yet in the search hit on many useful discoveries: so the preacher, applying his heart to know the work of God and despairing of finding it out, found something that recompensed him. What perplexed him was the little difference made between good and bad in the distribution of comforts and crosses; and before describing that temptation he lays down a truth to hold to. This has been the way of God’s people in the difficulty, he notes, each laying down some doctrine first; the truth fastened on here is that the righteous and the wise and their works are in the hand of God. They may seem given up to their enemies, but men have no power against them except what is given from above. Adam Clarke states the same soberly—they are protected by his power and safe in his approbation—while adding that we cannot judge from the occurrences of life who are the objects of God’s love or displeasure.

Whose love and hatred are meant is the sharpest question. Henry, John Wesley and Clarke take it of God’s: prosperity is no certain sign of his love nor affliction of his hatred, so that no man knows either by what is before him in this world. Henry adds that we may know it by what is within us, since if we love God with all our heart we may know that he loves us; Wesley makes it a rule that whom God loves he chastens and those he hates he often permits to prosper. Charles Ellicott disagrees. If the verse stood alone we should understand that a man cannot know whether he will meet with marks of divine favour or the reverse; but taking a later verse into account, he understands it of a man’s own love and hatred, whose objects he cannot tell beforehand. Keil and Delitzsch argue it more forcibly. The words are too general for the other sense: man is not their object here but their subject. Since he has not his actions in his own power, he does not know whether he will love or hate—which they admit sounds deterministic, and then defend. Is it not true, they ask, that love changes, without a man’s previous knowledge and by unexpected causes, into hatred, and hatred as unexpectedly into love? Neither is the product of self-determination.

On the one event that comes to all, the voices differ in temper rather than reading. John Gill says all outward things are shared alike by good and bad, which is what proves neither love nor hatred can be known from them, and cites a Roman emperor who reckoned life and death and honour and dishonour among things happening alike to both. Clarke grants the truth and qualifies it: God often does make a difference, and his followers witness many interventions of providence on their behalf, but there are general blessings and general natural evils that fall on just and unjust together. In this all is right; the evils in nature are effects of the Fall, God will not suspend general laws for individual cases, and every holy man has the testimony of God’s approbation in his own heart. There is evil enough to show that man has fallen and good enough to show that God deals with him in mercy, so he sees no rational cause to stumble at providence. Gill calls the equality of event a very great evil, though not as God’s providence is concerned in it, since God does no evil, but as it distresses good men and as bad men use it to harden themselves and despise religion. Keil and Delitzsch draw the same distinction: the author calls this not the greatest of evils but an evil mixed with all earthly events, a contradiction to the moral order and demoralising besides.
4:
The verse opens with a crux. John Gill notes that the written text gives chosen and the margin joined, the received version following the margin with the ancient translations. Charles Ellicott says the best sense the written form allows is to attach it to the previous verse and begin here, to all the living. Keil and Delitzsch are blunter: the written form admits no tenable meaning, and the proposal to render who has a choice? breaks the sequence. Adam Clarke offers his own attempt: what, therefore, is to be chosen? in him that is living there is hope. On the proverb Clarke supposes it was already current: the smallest measure of animal existence is better than the largest of dead matter, so that the poorest living peasant is infinitely above the greatest conqueror once he is dead. Matthew Henry puts it his own way, that the meanest beggar alive has the comfort of this world and does it the service which the greatest prince, being dead, is incapable of. Ellicott adds the detail that gives the saying its edge: apart from the shepherd’s dog and the watchdog, the dog is elsewhere an unclean animal, living or dead.

Henry draws two advantages from being alive. First, while there is life there is hope: if a man’s condition is bad there is hope it will be amended, and if his heart is full of evil there is hope that grace may work a blessed change, whereas afterwards it is too late, and he that is then filthy will be filthy still. Gill extends the hope to those called at the eleventh hour, even on a deathbed, and to any still under the means of grace; John Wesley says only that the living man has not merely present comfort but hope of further happiness in this world. Second, while there is life there is opportunity of preparing for death. The living know they shall die, and may be influenced by it to prepare for a change that comes certainly and may come suddenly; this, Henry says, is a needful knowledge, for what is our business while we live but to get ready to die—whereas the dead know they are dead, and it is too late. Gill marks the limits: death is the appointment of God and its time fixed, and even the wicked know they shall die though they put the evil day far off, yet no one knows the time or place of his own death.

How far the ignorance of the dead extends is handled carefully. Henry takes it of this world only and enumerates what ends: acquaintance, since it does not appear they know anything of what is done by those they leave behind; enjoyment, since what they got must be left to others, and the world can be an annuity for life but not a portion for ever; name, since the grave is a land of forgetfulness; and affection, since death parts those who loved and equally those who hated. Clarke states the limitation as a principle: the ignorance and want of power spoken of are in reference only to this life, and though the dead have no more a portion under the sun, he does not intimate they have none anywhere else. Gill goes further and denies the separate spirits are without affections at all, holding that love continues after this life and is then at its height, the passage respecting only things in this world. Wesley agrees that they are unconcerned in what is done under the sun, their memory forgotten even where they had lived in great power and glory. Keil and Delitzsch describe the tone rather than the doctrine: the account begins sarcastically, verifying the comparison just made, and then becomes elegiac; the reward they no longer have is a reward in this upper world, where it is too soon forgotten that they ever existed.
7:
The turn to enjoyment is not addressed to everyone. John Gill is careful about that: epicures and voluptuous persons stand in no need of such an exhortation, and the reason annexed to it does not suit them; the whole agrees better with religious persons who, under distressing views of Providence and gloomy apprehensions and mistaken notions of mortification, deny themselves the free and lawful use of the good things of life. Since there is no enjoyment of them in the grave, he says, let the advice be taken. Adam Clarke gives the same counsel more briefly: do not vex and perplex yourselves with the dispensations and mysteries of Providence, but enjoy the blessings God has given and live to his glory. Charles Ellicott notes that the ground offered has been given before in this book, that earthly enjoyment is to be received as a thing given by God’s favour, and that the acceptance spoken of is already settled rather than still to be earned.

The white garments and the oil are read as festal dress. Keil and Delitzsch set them against the black robes of mourning, and note that black and white were among the ancients colour-symbols of sorrow and joy, answering to darkness and light; fragrant oil belongs to the same class of heart-refreshing things, since sorrow and anointing exclude one another while joy and oil stand in the closest relation. They quote a rabbinic saying that catches the symbolism exactly: bury me neither in white nor in black—not in white, because perhaps I may not be one of the blessed, and should be like a bridegroom among mourners; not in black, because perhaps I may be one of the blessed, and should be like a mourner among bridegrooms. Gill takes the colour more plainly, of clothing neat and clean rather than vile and sordid, comely and decent and suitable to a man’s circumstances, and explains why the colour is named: it was much used in those countries, whence the frequent washing of garments and the trade of the fullers who whitened them, and especially on days of rejoicing. The sense he draws is that every day should be like a festival to a good man, though there may be times for mourning and other apparel. Clarke says the same of festal occasions, where the white was an emblem of joy and innocence, adds that whole populations in the East go clothed in clean white cotton, and sums the verse as be always pure and always happy. John Wesley confirms the custom, that people of the better sort in those countries wore white especially in times of rejoicing, and that ointment was poured on the head upon joyful occasions. Gill and Clarke both record the older allegorical readings alongside the plain one—garments kept pure from the stain of sin, an unblemished conversation, repentance and good works, and a good name likened to the oil of anointing, that blessings may be called down upon the head.
9:
The counsel to live joyfully with a wife is read as sober advice rather than licence. John Gill makes it one of the principal ways of enjoying life comfortably—a man ought to love his wife as his own flesh, take delight in her company, be pleasant with her and rejoice in her—and takes the clause to stand for all the lawful satisfaction to be had in the enjoyment of other relations and friends, which adds no small part to the comfort of a man’s life. Adam Clarke renders it as three counsels together: marry prudently, keep faithfully attached to the wife thou hast chosen, and rejoice in the labour of thy hands. He records that some understand the words as the speech of a libertine objector, live joyfully with the woman thou lovest best, but judges that this does not comport so well with the scope of the place. Keil and Delitzsch rest an argument on the grammar. Most translators render the wife whom thou lovest, but the author purposely uses the indefinite forms of both nouns, so that the sense is rather to bring into experience what life and happiness are with a wife whom one has loved—in which there lies indirectly a call to choose such a one. They add that on this reading the pessimistic estimate of women made earlier in the book falls into the background, the happier side of the author’s view of the world predominating here.

The exhortation that follows keeps the counsel from becoming idleness. Keil and Delitzsch say so explicitly: the author recommends no continual doing of nothing, no useless sluggard’s life devoted to pleasure, but gives his exhortation to joy its converse side, that all a man’s hand may reach to accomplish he should do. They find the accentuation ingenious, since had the author meant simply do it with all thy might he would have written otherwise; as the words stand they call on a man to fall short of no possibility within the measure of his strength, that is, to work straining his capacity to the uttermost. John Wesley gives the same sense in a line: whatever a man has opportunity and ability to do, let him do it with unwearied diligence and vigour and expedition. Gill enters one restriction, that what is meant is not anything evil, which is always near at hand and easy to find, but whatsoever is good. Clarke expands the verse into a threefold examination of what, how and why. What is necessary to be done in this life with reference to another he sets out as a course—to turn from sin and repent, to frequent the ordinances of God and keep company with the upright, to read the Scriptures and pray for pardon, to believe, to look for the gift of the Spirit and bring forth its fruits in their seasons, to live to get good and to do good, and to refer every purpose and act to the eternal world. How it is to be done is with thy might: be fully convinced of the necessity of these things, be determined to act according to that conviction, and then act with all thy strength. Why it is to be done he grounds on the clause following: because thou art a dying man, and when thou leavest this life thy state of probation with all its advantages is eternally ended, so that in the grave there is no work by which thou mayest profit, no device by which thou mayest escape, no knowledge of any means of help and no wisdom to restore thee. Charles Ellicott adds only that the grave named here is Sheol.
11:
Matthew Henry sets the observation against the exhortation just given: we were told to do what we have to do with all our might, and are reminded that when we have done all we must leave the issue with God. He gives four instances, each introduced by what one would naturally expect. One would think the lightest of foot should win the race, yet some accident retards them, or they grow remiss and let slower men get the start. One would think the more powerful army should always be victorious, yet a host of Philistines was once put to flight by Jonathan and his armour-bearer, and a good cause has often carried the day against the most formidable power. One would think men of sense should be men of substance, yet many who seemed likely to thrive have strangely gone backward; and those who understand men should get preferment, yet many have spent their days in obscurity, or ruined themselves by the very methods by which they hoped to rise. Henry resolves these disappointments into an over-ruling providence whose disposals seem casual, so that we call them chance, though they follow the determinate counsel of God, here called time. A sovereign Providence breaks men’s measures and blasts their hopes, teaching them that the way of man is not in himself; we must use means but not trust them, giving God the praise if we succeed and acquiescing if we are crossed.

John Gill draws the same conclusion, that men should promise themselves nothing from their own strength and wisdom, but have regard to the providence of God, who gives or withholds success as he pleases. Adam Clarke puts it as a rule about confidence: it is not by swiftness, nor by strength and valour, that races are gained and battles won, and no man should confide in himself. He then takes the two nouns of the last clause apart. Every man has time to act in, and an opportunity of doing some particular work; but within that opportunity there is incident, what may fall in, and occurrence, what may meet and frustrate an attempt—so while you have time seek an opportunity of doing what is right, and yet calculate on hindrances. Keil and Delitzsch rest on the grammar: the preposition repeated five times is that of ownership, by virtue of which a man is master of a thing and disposes of it freely, so that the race does not belong to the swift, their fleetness being no guarantee. Charles Ellicott notes only that the word rendered chance occurs elsewhere but once.

The second verse turns to unforeseen calamity. Keil and Delitzsch state the principle: the particular has its reason from the general, since man is not master of his own time, person or life, and therefore not of the fruits of his capabilities, in spite of favourable conditions that appear to put the result beyond doubt. Gill says that although the time is fixed by the Lord, times and seasons are kept in his own power and not known by men—neither the time of his death, nor of any calamity coming on him, nor the proper season for doing himself good. John Wesley understands the time of death or other distress God is bringing, and observes that the creatures are taken while sporting and feeding, when they are most careless and secure. Clarke presses the comparison home: man acts so heedlessly, for all his wisdom and warnings, that he is taken as a fish by the baited hook and a bird by the snare, and the evil time falls on him suddenly, so that he is taken in a moment with no means of escaping. Henry sets this beside the first half of the passage—we are often disappointed of the good we had great hopes of, and as often surprised by the evils we were in little fear of.
13:
The story is told for a wisdom that goes unrewarded. Matthew Henry defines it: the wisdom that seemed great to the preacher is that which enables a man to serve his country out of pure affection when he gains no advantage by it, not so much as thanks or the reputation of it—a public spirit in a private sphere. He is careful that the earlier saying, that bread is not always to the wise, not be taken as disparagement: wisdom still excels folly as light excels darkness, and is to be embraced for its own worth though it never enrich us. John Wesley says it is added for the commendation of wisdom, notwithstanding its insufficiency for happiness without God’s blessing. John Gill notes that the preacher, having spoken of how little success attends the wise, observes that wisdom exists among men nevertheless; Keil and Delitzsch insist the sentence must not be broken up, the sense being that in this incident too he saw wisdom of exceeding greatness.

Whether the incident happened is disputed. Gill reports that some take it for history, as the city of Abel was delivered by a wise woman’s counsel, while others hold it a parable whose moral is that political wisdom in a poor man is serviceable and yet unrewarded. Charles Ellicott calls the search for a historical reference idle: what is told is so like the deliverance of Abel-beth-Maachah by a wise woman whose name was likewise not preserved that we cannot be sure the writer had another history in mind. Henry treats it as a case in fact: the city was no great prize, and had few men to defend it—men, if men of fortitude, being the best fortifications of a city; against it a great king came in pride or covetousness or revenge, and built bulwarks he did not need.

The allegorical readings divide the voices. Gill records the Jewish interpretation in which the little city is the body, the few men the righteousness in the heart, the great king the corruption of nature besieging it, and the poor wise man the better imagination; and he offers a Christian allegory, taking the poor wise man for Christ. Adam Clarke reports the same Jewish allegory and rejects both outright: those who spiritualise the passage, making the little city the Church, the few men the apostles, the great king the devil and the poor wise man Christ, abuse the text. What he offers instead is the defence of Syracuse, where Archimedes destroyed ships with burning-glasses and lifted galleys from the water with his machines, so that one man’s wisdom long prevailed against a mighty nation, and the city fell at last to treachery rather than force.

The neglect that follows is the point. Henry observes that the man was wise and yet preferred to no place of profit or power; that being wise he served the city notwithstanding, without upbraiding them for leaving him out of their council, from which Henry draws that private resentments must be sacrificed to the common welfare; and that being poor he was slighted afterwards, so that many who have well merited of their country have been ill paid, such an ungrateful world do we live in. Wesley says he was soon neglected and his great service forgotten. Keil and Delitzsch explain why. Wisdom is better than strength because it does more for the wise man, and through him for others, than force can; but the respect wisdom secures sinks, in a poor man, into the contempt his poverty exposes him to. In an emergency his service is valued; as a rule his words are unheeded, the crowd estimating a man by the outward respect he is held in. Clarke ends on the same note, with the soldier who found Archimedes drawing figures in the sand, was told to stand off and not spoil the diagram, and struck him dead.
17:
The proverb about quiet words is read two ways. John Gill gives both: either the words of wise men are in fact heard in quiet by some persons and at some times, though not by all and not always, or—the sense he thinks the comparison requires—they are delivered in quiet, with a low and submissive voice, without noise or blustering pride or passion, sedately and with great humility, submitted to the judgment of others. Either way, he adds, they ought to be heard patiently and without tumult or contradiction, even when the speaker is poor. John Wesley settles on the second: the words are uttered with a modest and low voice, and what they are set against is the clamorous discourse of a rich and potent but foolish man. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by argument. The contrast between quiet and cry requires us to attribute the tranquillity to the wise man himself and not to his hearers, against the reading that makes it a matter of how he is listened to; and the second phrase does not mean a ruler over fools, which would leave it doubtful whether he were not a fool himself, but a ruler among fools, one who takes the chief place among them—as elsewhere a man is called a ruler among men or the lion the hero among beasts. Adam Clarke keeps to the illustration he has been pursuing: in the tumult of war the words of Archimedes were not heard, and his life was lost.

The last verse turns the story into a proverb and then undercuts it. Gill takes the first half straightforwardly, that wisdom does what weapons cannot, of which the poor wise man is full proof, since he delivered the city from a potent prince when weapons of war could not. Keil and Delitzsch say the proverb leans on the history just narrated, wisdom accomplishing more than all the apparatus belonging to preparation for war; but they treat the two halves as a synthetic pair whose parts may be interpreted independently, so that as wisdom accomplishes something great, a single villain may have an influence just as far-reaching. The much good a wise man is accomplishing or has accomplished may be rendered vain by one sinner through treachery or calumny, or destroyed through mere malicious pleasure in evil. Clarke applies both halves to his own example—wisdom better than weapons, as was proved at Syracuse, and the good destroyed being the life and skill of the mathematician, cut off by the soldier who did not know him—and then generalises. One sinner has often injured the work of God, and one stumbling-block has sometimes destroyed a revival of religion; sin acts like a ferment, assimilating to itself whatever comes in contact with it.
